issues.legal_issue: A transfer made while litigation concerning the property is pending is not void merely because it is pendente lite, but the transferee is bound by the result of that litigation.
material_facts: The owner transferred the land to a purchaser while a suit concerning ownership of the land was pending.
The lower courts treated the transfer as hit by the doctrine of lis pendens.
issues.conclusion: The transfer was not rendered void or ineffective merely by the pending litigation; the purchaser remained bound by the result of that litigation.
issues.legal_principle: Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 prohibits a transfer during pending litigation from defeating the rights determined in that litigation, but does not itself declare the transfer void.

predicates.civil_appeal_concerning_a_transfer_durin: The proceeding is a civil appeal concerning a transfer made while a property dispute was pending.
predicates.transfer_made_during_pending_suit: The property was transferred while a suit concerning it was pending.
predicates.pending_suit_determines_rights_in_proper: The pending suit concerns the rights in the property transferred.

issues.definition: When a civil appeal concerns a transfer made during a pending property suit that determines rights in the property, the transfer remains effective but is subject to the suit's outcome.

issues.legal_issue: A transferee for consideration may elect to claim an interest that the transferor later acquires when the transfer was made on a representation of authority, the contract remains subsisting, and the transfer was not invalid under law; the requirements of good faith and reasonable care applicable to an ostensible-owner transfer do not govern that claim.
material_facts: The transferor sold the land for consideration while litigation over the land was pending.
The transfer was not held void or contrary to law merely because it occurred during the litigation.
The transferor later became entitled, through succession, to an interest in the land.
There was no finding that the purchaser knew the transferor lacked title; knowledge of pending litigation was not treated as equivalent to such knowledge.
The purchaser's claim was supported under the rule concerning a transferor who later acquires the interest purportedly transferred.
issues.conclusion: Section 43 applied to the transfer, allowing the purchaser to claim the interest the transferor later acquired. The purchaser did not have to satisfy the good-faith and reasonable-care requirements of Section 41 merely because those requirements apply to a transfer by an ostensible owner.
issues.legal_principle: Section 43 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 embodies the rule of feeding the estoppel: where a competent contracting transferor fraudulently or erroneously represents authority and transfers property for consideration, the transferee may, at their option, claim an interest the transferor later acquires if the contract is then subsisting. The transfer must not be invalid under law or contrary to public policy under Section 23 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, and a later good-faith transferee for value without notice is protected. Unlike Section 41, Section 43 does not require the transferee to establish good faith and reasonable care. Jumma Masjid, Mercara v. Kodimaniandra Deviah, AIR 1962 SC 847, explains the breadth of Section 43 and the rule of feeding the estoppel. Kartar Singh v. Harbans Kaur, (1994) 4 SCC 730, concerned an alienation that was void as to a minor's share and a contract that could not subsist; N. Srinivasa Rao v. Special Court under the A.P. Land Grabbing (Prohibition) Act, (2006) 4 SCC 214, concerned an invalid transfer. Neither controlled a transaction that was not invalid under law.

rule.if: civil_appeal_concerning_a_transferee_claim_to_later_acquired_property and transfer_for_consideration_on_representation and transferee_relied_on_representation and transfer_contract_remained_subsisting and transferor_later_acquired_interest and transfer_not_invalid_under_law and not subsequent_good_faith_purchaser_without_notice

predicates.civil_appeal_concerning_a_transferee_cla: The proceeding is a civil appeal concerning a transferee's claim to an interest later acquired by the transferor.
predicates.transfer_for_consideration_on_representa: The transferor represented authority to transfer the property and purported to transfer it for consideration.
predicates.transferee_relied_on_representation: The transferee took the transfer on the faith of the transferor's representation.
predicates.transfer_contract_remained_subsisting: The contract of transfer remained subsisting when the transferee claimed the property.
predicates.transferor_later_acquired_interest: The transferor acquired an interest in the property after making the transfer.
predicates.transfer_not_invalid_under_law: The transfer was not invalid because it was forbidden by law or contrary to public policy.
predicates.subsequent_good_faith_purchaser_without_: A later purchaser acquired the property for value in good faith and without notice of the earlier transferee's option.

issues.definition: If a civil appeal concerns a transferee who relied on a representation in a subsisting, for-consideration transfer, and the transferor later acquires the interest without the transfer being invalid under law or a protected later purchaser intervening, the transferee may elect to claim that interest.

issues.legal_issue: A claimant relying on an unproved will cannot use the transferor's objection to the application of the rule of feeding the estoppel to establish the claimant's own title; absent proof of the will, title is governed by general succession and inheritance law.
material_facts: The claimant asserted an absolute interest in the property on the basis of a will said to have been executed by the prior owner.
The will was not proved in accordance with the applicable requirements for proof of a will.
The claimant, rather than the transferor who made the sale, sought to raise the objection that the rule of feeding the estoppel did not apply.
issues.conclusion: The will did not establish the claimant's asserted title; general succession and inheritance law applied, and the claimant could not raise the transferor's objection to the application of the rule of feeding the estoppel.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 and 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 govern proof of a will. Where the will is not proved, the general law of succession and inheritance applies. The Court held that the objection to the application of Section 43 could have been taken by the transferor, but not by a claimant whose title was asserted on the basis of the unproved will.

rule.if: civil_appeal_concerning_title_claimed_through_a_will and claimant_based_title_on_will and will_not_proved and claimant_is_not_the_transferor

predicates.civil_appeal_concerning_title_claimed_th: The proceeding is a civil appeal in which title is claimed through a will.
predicates.claimant_based_title_on_will: The claimant relied on a will as the basis for the claimed title.
predicates.will_not_proved: The will was not proved in accordance with the applicable evidentiary requirements.
predicates.claimant_is_not_the_transferor: The person raising the objection is not the person who made the transfer.

issues.definition: Where a claimant in a civil appeal bases title on an unproved will and is not the transferor, the will does not establish that title and the claimant cannot raise the transferor's estoppel objection.
